headline: High: Flowise’s broad egress and file access can leak or mis-handle content when paired with an unverified content-writing agent, while shared-state orchestration raises conflict and cascade risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A is a content-writing agent with no documented shared channel to B, while B can read/write files and run browser/tool nodes. The only plausible bridge is manual or file-based transfer, so injection is possible but not default. Because A is unverified and B’s tool parsing is flow-driven, uncertainty stays on the higher side of low.
conditions: IF A’s output is copied into a Flowise node or uploaded file that B parses as instructions
IF B’s flow includes a prompt/template node that consumes A-authored text without sanitization
mitigations: Use a strict delimiter/template for any copied text
Disable auto-ingest of uploaded files into prompt nodes
Add a provenance label to A-generated content
Review flows for instruction-following nodes before execution

B_data_leakage.rationale: B explicitly touches chatflow inputs/outputs, uploaded files, and model-provider/tool credentials, and has broad network egress. A is a content-writing agent with broad egress but no filesystem surface documented. The pair can therefore move sensitive chatflow content into external APIs in default Flowise-style deployments, making leakage plausible without extra setup.
conditions: IF chatflow inputs contain secrets, customer data, or uploaded files
IF a flow sends those inputs to model providers or HTTP/search tools
mitigations: Remove secrets from chatflow inputs
Restrict flows to approved model providers only
Turn off file upload nodes for sensitive runs
Add a pre-run checklist for data-class review
Rotate any exposed credentials immediately

C_capability_conflict.rationale: B can write the filesystem and shares state across instances via server datastore; A has broad network egress and may emit content that B stores or reuses. Even though A has no write surface documented, the pair still conflicts on shared mutable chatflow artifacts and external side effects. Uncertainty about A’s runtime pushes this above low.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same workspace or datastore-backed flow artifacts
IF A’s outputs are persisted by B while another B instance is running
mitigations: Assign separate workspaces per run
Serialize writes to shared flow artifacts
Disable concurrent edits during execution
Snapshot flow state before running
Use a lock file or datastore mutex

D_cascading_error.rationale: B’s graph-based flows can treat upstream node output as authoritative, and A is a content-writing agent whose outputs may be consumed as facts or instructions. That creates a default cascade path from A’s text into B’s downstream actions. Because B can call APIs and browsers, the blast radius can extend beyond a single document.
conditions: IF B uses A’s output as an input node without verification
IF downstream nodes send emails, API calls, or browser actions based on that output
mitigations: Insert a verification node between A and action nodes
Require human approval before external side effects
Constrain downstream nodes to read-only mode
Add schema checks for A’s outputs
Log and review all action-triggering prompts

E_compliance.rationale: B explicitly handles chatflow inputs/outputs, model keys, and tool credentials, while A is an unverified open-source content-writing agent with broad egress. The pair does not show a specific residency regime, so I cannot claim a higher breach class; however, the documented handling of secrets and external calls creates a realistic compliance mismatch risk around retention and third-party transfer.
conditions: IF regulated data is entered into Flowise chatflows
IF logs or provider calls retain prompts, outputs, or uploaded files beyond policy
mitigations: Block regulated data from these flows
Set short log-retention windows
Review provider DPAs before use
Document data-flow and residency boundaries
Purge stored chatflow artifacts after testing
